title: Can I Convince You to Be a Tiny Bit Robot-Curious
author: Curious Pedagogy
summary: A biology professor recounts teaching an upper-division Developmental Biology seminar where the core skill is critically reading dense primary scientific literature, and describes a deliberate effort to move students beyond blanket AI skepticism toward skillful, bounded AI use. Building on a colleague's introductory-level assignment that successfully generated productive AI distrust through a social 'pile-on' dynamic, the author designed an AI policy explicitly permitting AI as a research collaborator while holding students fully responsible for submitted content, and modeled AI-assisted literature search using tools like Elicit, Semantic Scholar, and NotebookLM. The piece candidly reports a surprising public/private split: in class, students performed AI abstinence in front of peers, disdaining classmates who used it too much, while privately in office hours the same students asked for AI demonstrations and used AI-generated tools like concept maps and flowcharts to support their reading. The author connects this to the fact that the introductory exercise worked precisely because rejecting AI became a shared, social activity, a dynamic that could not be replicated for genuine adoption of a tool. The piece closes with concrete prompts the author shared with students for using AI to responsibly search academic literature, including explicit verification instructions.
points: Documents a striking public/private split in student AI attitudes: uniform public disdain for AI use in class discussion, but active, curious requests for AI demonstrations (search strategies, concept maps, flowcharts) during private office hours.

Distinguishes 'deployed unskillfully' AI reading of scientific papers, which draws conclusions from word order rather than the data and images the words describe, from AI used as a bounded research collaborator under an explicit accountability policy.

Explains why an introductory-level 'hate AI together' assignment worked pedagogically: it succeeded because rejecting AI became a shared social act, a dynamic that cannot be manufactured for genuine skill-building adoption.

Provides a specific AI syllabus policy template treating generative AI like permitted group work: usable as a collaborator, but the student remains fully responsible for submitted content regardless of AI involvement.

Supplies concrete, reusable prompts for using AI to kick off academic literature searches, paired with an explicit instruction to verify every AI-suggested source against a traditional search engine before relying on it.
quotes: Deployed unskillfully, an LLM reads a paper like an undergraduate student: it draws conclusions from the order of the authors' words, not from the images and data the authors are describing.

Generative AI tools can be a powerful help in approaching the scientific literature, and we will explore how to effectively use AI as a collaborator in your reading and exploration of your topics. However, as with group work, when you put your name on an assignment for which you've had help from generative AI, you are responsible for the content.

In class, in front of their peers, AI abstinence ruled. Students expressed concerns about AI energy use and intellectual property. They disdained students (in other classes, of course) who used AI too much.
Whereas in class, the frustration and disdain that George's 100-level students showed for using AI as a learning substitute was on full display, in a one on one setting, students were more curious.
